summary: This informational RFC describes how unexpected traffic flows can appear across an autonomous system when other networks filter or restrict propagation of more-specific prefixes. It reviews ways to detect that issue and defend against it.

eli5.summary: If some roads are hidden from the map, drivers take detours through places you never planned for. This explains why that happens and how to spot it.

questions: how to detect unexpected traffic flows
subtitle: How prefix filtering can create unexpected network traffic patterns

tldr.problem: When some networks filter or restrict propagation of more-specific IP prefixes, traffic meant for those prefixes can unexpectedly flow through other networks that still have routes for them, violating the filtering network's traffic policies.
tldr.mechanism: Routers forward packets using longest-prefix-match, which can override BGP policies. When a network filters a more-specific prefix, packets for that prefix still match the less-specific prefix and get forwarded elsewhere, potentially traversing networks they should not.
tldr.outcome: This document explains the problem, shows how to detect it using flow monitoring tools, and recommends reactive approaches (peer communication and reactive filtering) over complex proactive solutions.

today: RFC 7789 remains a current informational reference for operators dealing with inter-domain routing anomalies caused by prefix filtering. It has not been obsoleted and continues to describe a real operational problem in BGP networks.

sections.title: The Filtering Problem
sections.content:
Network operators commonly advertise both a less-specific IP prefix and more-specific prefixes within it. A less-specific prefix of 2001:db8::/32 might be paired with 2001:db8::/34, which is more specific.

This creates a mismatch when some networks filter the more-specific prefix. Although BGP policies should decide which network path to use, routers must forward packets using the longest-prefix-match rule from RFC 1812. This means a packet destined for the more-specific prefix will be forwarded according to that more-specific route, even when policies would have chosen a different path for the less-specific prefix. As a result, traffic can flow through networks in ways their operators never intended.
sections.eli5: You can set rules for which roads cars should take, but cars always follow the longest, most specific route they know. So if you hide a specific road, cars still take it if they know about it from somewhere else.

sections.title: Two Types of Filtering
sections.content:
Local filtering happens when a network explicitly blocks a more-specific prefix on its own border. This might be for traffic engineering (to control outbound traffic distribution), to enforce peering agreements, or to save router memory. The RFC illustrates a case where AS64504 filters the more-specific prefix 2001:db8::/34 to prefer sending traffic through a less-expensive settlement-free peer rather than a paid transit provider.

Remote filtering uses BGP communities, which are tags that tell distant networks not to propagate a prefix to certain peers. A network can ask its provider to announce the more-specific prefix only to a specific neighbor, rather than everywhere. Remote filtering is more subtle because the restriction originates with a distant AS.
sections.eli5: Local filtering is when you block a road at your own border. Remote filtering is when you ask someone far away to hide a road on their side.

sections.title: Examples of Unexpected Traffic
sections.content:
The RFC provides detailed scenarios. In one, AS64504 filters a more-specific prefix locally. This causes its traffic to take an alternative path through AS64502. However, AS64502 receives the more-specific prefix from AS64503, a peer whose traffic AS64502 is not supposed to carry. Packets now traverse AS64502 between two peers that should not exchange traffic according to AS64502's policies.

In another scenario using remote filtering, AS64501 asks AS64503 to limit propagation of a more-specific prefix. This causes upstream networks like AS64505 that never received the more-specific prefix to forward packets for it using the less-specific route. Those packets end up at AS64502, which has the more-specific route and delivers them through unexpected paths.
sections.eli5: When you hide a specific road, drivers use the next-best route they know. But that might send them through someone else's neighborhood by accident, breaking their traffic rules.

sections.title: Detecting Unexpected Flows
sections.content:
Operators can detect unexpected traffic flows using flow monitoring and collection systems. Tools like IPFIX (RFC 7011) export flow data, and open-source software like pmacct can combine flow statistics with business relationship information to identify flows that violate policy.

The first step is to check local BGP configuration for errors. If the configuration is correct, the operator should determine whether a neighbor is forwarding based on a less-specific prefix while the affected network holds a more-specific path from a non-customer. This indicates the neighbor may have filtered the more-specific prefix. Identifying the cause of the filter (local, remote, or selective propagation) requires human investigation and looking glass tools, as no automatic detection method is widely available.
sections.eli5: You can see unusual traffic patterns by watching what actually flows through your network. First check your own rules are right. Then ask neighbors if they blocked certain roads.

sections.title: Responding to the Problem
sections.content:
The RFC recommends a reactive approach over proactive solutions. When unexpected flows are detected, operators should contact the responsible networks and ask them to change their behavior.

If direct contact fails, an operator can implement its own filtering. It can either stop announcing the less-specific prefix to the problematic neighbor (which loses some traffic) or filter the more-specific prefix upon receipt (which may create conflicts with the originating network).

The RFC discourages proactive solutions like access lists or neighbor-specific forwarding because they are operationally complex, have high overhead, and can drop legitimate traffic from neighbors unaware of the policy conflict. Deploying VRF routing tables to enforce per-neighbor forwarding decisions is technically possible but operationally burdensome.
sections.eli5: The best fix is to talk to the other network and ask them to stop. Blocking their traffic yourself works but is complicated and might cause other problems. Complex tricks to prevent it are not worth the effort.
